title: Singing together
hookLine: in adult classes, people who sang together bonded faster than people in other classes (Pearce et al.)

lines: BY THE LAST LINE, THE ROOM IS TOGETHER.
cards: Nobody sings happy birthday well. The room starts in several keys at once, someone goes too high on the name, the candles drip wax on the frosting. And yet, by the last line, the room is together.
People who were strangers when they walked in are laughing at the same off note. It would be easy to say that's just the cake.
A team of researchers wondered whether singing itself does something to strangers, and how fast. Here's what they found, and the honest limits of it.

teach.b: First, the classes. Eiluned Pearce, Jacques Launay and Robin Dunbar followed adult education classes, the kind people sign up for to learn something new. Some classes sang together.
Others did crafts or creative writing. Second, the measure.
At points through the course, people rated how close they felt to their classmates.
Third, the finding: the singers bonded faster. Early on, people in the singing classes felt closer to each other than people in the other classes did, as if singing broke the ice.
The authors called it an ice-breaker effect. Fourth, the honest part.
Over the months, the other classes caught up. Crafts and writing made friends too; it just took longer. So singing isn't magic.
It may be a shortcut to a place people reach in other ways. Traditions already sing together: hymns in churches, kirtan in Sikh gurdwaras, bhajans in Hindu temples, psalms sung in synagogues.

teach.h: LET US MAKE A JOYFUL NOISE.
teach.b: One psalm opens with an invitation to sing as a group, in the King James words: "O come, let us sing unto the LORD: let us make a joyful noise to the rock of our salvation." Notice the word us.
And a joyful noise doesn't ask for good voices. It asks for voices together.

how: Congregations in several traditions sing together: hymns in churches, kirtan in Sikh gurdwaras, bhajans in Hindu temples, psalms and prayers sung in synagogues.

games.q: you join an adult evening class full of strangers. the choices: singing, crafts, or creative writing. in the study, which group felt close fastest?
games.why: the singers bonded fastest at first. over the months, the crafts and writing classes caught up.

practice: Choose a tune you know without thinking, a lullaby, a hymn, a song from a car ride long ago, and hum a line or two quietly, feeling where the sound buzzes: lips, nose, chest. If someone is near you, hum it with them.
Then stop, and sit in the quiet the hum leaves behind.

wordCard.voice: Singing together. In a study of adult classes, the people who sang together felt close faster than the others, who caught up later. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew, from Psalm 95:1: "let us sing," a call to sing out together.

carryVoice: Your line: sing together. Off-key counts; the psalm asks for a joyful noise, not a perfect one. See you tomorrow.
